title: Event Handling
body:
[[Event Object]]
[[Event Propagation]] and [[Event Delegation]]

---

Attaching a function to a node so the browser runs it when something happens to that node.

```js
node.addEventListener("click", (e) => { ... });
```

Three arguments' worth of decisions: **which event** (`click`, `change`, `input`, `submit`,
`keydown`, `mouseover`), **which node** listens, and **what the handler does**. The second one
is the interesting question, and [[Event Propagation]] is why the answer is often not the node
the user actually clicked.

`addEventListener` is preferred over the old `node.onclick = fn` because several listeners can
coexist on one node; assigning `onclick` twice silently replaces the first. Inline
`onclick="..."` attributes in the [[HTML]] are worse again, since they put behaviour back in
the markup that [[CSS]] and JS exist to keep it out of.

The handler is a [[Call Back Function]]: you do not call it, the browser does, at some point
in the future. That is also why [[This]] inside a `function` handler is the node, and inside
an [[Arrow Syntax]] handler is not.

See [[DOM + Event Handling]] for where this sits in a script.
